questions.stem: A graph of input styles uses (hover: hover); what does it test?

options.text: Whether the primary input can hover

questions.explanation: (hover: hover) tests whether the primary input mechanism can hover. Touch-only, animation, and width are separate features. Each media feature tests one condition.

questions.topic: Breaking a tie between equally specific rules
questions.stem: What is the specificity of the universal selector * in a graph of rules?
questions.explanation: The universal selector has zero specificity. It never wins a tie on its own. Counting it as element or class overstates its weight.

options.text: The smallest size that fits the content

questions.topic: A fixed track beside a fractional one
questions.stem: A grid track is minmax(0, 200px) beside a 1fr track in a 400px container; what is the max track width?

questions.topic: Weighted shrinking along a flex line
questions.stem: Explain how flex-shrink behaves when flex-basis is auto in a flex item shown in a graph.

answer.exemplar: With flex-basis auto, the basis is the item's content size, and shrink is weighted by shrink factor times that content size. Larger content loses more space proportionally.

questions.explanation: auto basis uses content size as the starting point. Shrink weighting multiplies factor by that basis. Ignoring content size miscomputes shrink.

questions.topic: Counting the elements a descendant selector reaches
questions.stem: How many elements does :only-child match in a container with a single paragraph in a graph?
questions.explanation: :only-child matches an element that is the only child of its parent. With one paragraph, it matches that paragraph. It does not need siblings or match all.

questions.stem: In a single-line flex container, what does align-content do in a graph?

options.text: It aligns items along the main axis
It has no effect because there is only one line
It wraps items onto new lines

questions.topic: Breaking a tie between equally specific rules
questions.stem: Explain why an ID selector beats a class selector in a graph of competing rules.

answer.exemplar: An ID selector has higher specificity than a class selector, so when both target the same element the ID rule wins. Specificity ranking places IDs above classes and elements.

questions.explanation: ID specificity (1,0,0) outranks class specificity (0,1,0). The cascade uses this ranking to choose the winner. Equal or lower specificity would lose.
